first.rationale: The two observed declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are internal funnel problems, and the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue rather than short-term volume. memory_86 and memory_31 converge on the same causal lever (less friction early in the funnel produces durable completion and activation lift), which makes simplify_onboarding the best-supported direct remedy; memory_91 (activation messaging) is a plausible second but treats a symptom further downstream than where the drop starts. I am deliberately not chasing promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73's summary reports 'acquisition and revenue lift' with no indication that it tracked retained or qualified revenue, and discount-led SMB acquisition is exactly the case where a headline win can mask degraded downstream account value and anchor price expectations. enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) does not address either declining metric this week. I am spending my single verification pull on memory_86 rather than memory_73 because memory_86 is the memory my chosen action actually rests on: these are consolidated summaries with sources archived, stripped of effect sizes, segment scope, and duration, so I need to know whether the reported adoption lift persisted into retained qualified revenue or whether shortening onboarding merely moved users past a step while reducing setup quality and later value. All inherited findings here are pre-competitor-entry (days 12-52) and the current environment has shifted, so I treat their magnitudes as unverified priors, not settled effect sizes. Running at standard experiment scale with holdout, and instrumenting not just completion/activation but downstream 30-60 day retention and qualified-revenue-per-account, so that a friction-reduction win that quietly lowers account value is detectable before any broad rollout.

final.rationale: The archive confirms memory_86 with the detail the summary had lost: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and critically 30-day retention +3%. That last figure is what I was worried about \u2014 it rules out the main failure mode where reduced friction just pushes users past a step while degrading setup quality and downstream value. The lift went the right direction on retention, not just on the funnel metric being optimized. Combined with memory_31's independently consistent finding on signup simplification, this is now the best-evidenced lever I have, and it targets the actual observed declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) at the point in the funnel where they originate rather than downstream. Remaining uncertainty I am not papering over: 30-day retention is a proxy for, not a measurement of, sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and exp_86 predates the competitor's entry pricing, so its effect size may not transfer to a market where price-sensitive SMBs now have a cheap alternative. Reducing onboarding friction also does nothing directly about the competitive price pressure; I am accepting that because promotional_pricing (memory_73) remains unverified on exactly the dimension that matters \u2014 its summary reports acquisition and revenue lift with no evidence it tracked retained or qualified revenue \u2014 and discount-led acquisition risks anchoring price expectations and importing low-value accounts, which cuts against the stated long-term objective. Running at standard experiment scale with a holdout rather than broad rollout, since the confirming record is a single pre-shift study. Instrumenting completion and activation as primary, plus 30/60/90-day retention and qualified-revenue-per-account as guardrails, with a pre-committed stop if per-account value drops even while completion rises. If it holds under current market conditions, that justifies broader rollout next cycle and frees a later slot to test the pricing question properly.
